summary: The Path Computation Element (PCE) is a core component of software-defined networking. This document specifies Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) procedures and extensions for using the PCE as a central controller (PCECC) that provisions labels along the path of a static Label Switched Path, so that a central server can download label-forwarding entries to each device on the path.

eli5.summary: Instead of every road sign being set by a different worker, one boss decides the signs and sends them out. This document lets a central computer tell each router what labels to use on a path.

questions: pcep extensions for static lsp label provisioning
what is a pce central controller
how does pcep set up a static lsp
what is the cci object in pcep
subtitle: How a central PCE server can tell every router on a static MPLS path which labels to use.

tldr.problem: A static label switched path needs explicit label-forwarding instructions on every router along it, and setting these up box by box is slow and hard to keep consistent.
tldr.mechanism: The PCE acts as a central controller. It uses PCEP, with a new Path Setup Type 2, a PCECC capability sub-TLV and a new CCI object, to download label instructions to each router on the path, and it can also have a router allocate its own labels.
tldr.outcome: A controller can calculate, set up, update and clean up an LSP end to end, reusing the existing stateful PCE machinery. The RFC is updated by RFC 9756.

today: RFC 9050 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9756. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: A PCE as a Central Controller
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) was developed to take path computation off routers in an MPLS traffic-engineered network. Routers acting as Path Computation Clients (PCCs) talk to it using the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP). Over time the PCE gained delegated control and PCE-initiated LSPs, and the SDN view of a central controller that programs devices fits what a PCE already does.

This RFC specifies procedures and PCEP extensions for using the PCE as a central controller (PCECC) for static LSPs. Each LSP is provisioned as explicit label instructions at each hop. The controller keeps a view of the network, decides the end-to-end paths and uses PCEP to talk to every router on the path.

The approach blends elements of SDN into a distributed control plane without necessarily replacing it. The RFC says its encodings are built so extensions for other cases are easy; Segment Routing extensions are mentioned as separate work.
sections.eli5: Normally each router picks its own signs. Here one smart helper plans the whole route and tells every router what sign to put up.

sections.title: The Basic PCECC Mode
sections.content:
In the basic PCECC mode, the PCE-based controller takes responsibility for managing part of the MPLS label space on each router it controls. A PCC MUST NOT allocate from the label space set aside for the PCE, which avoids overlaps and collisions. It is RECOMMENDED that the PCE allocates labels for all nodes along the path.

The RFC assumes the exclusive label range used by a PCE is known and set on both PCEP peers. Advertising it through PCEP is left to a possible future extension.

A second case is also allowed: the PCC keeps the label space and allocates the labels itself, with the PCE asking for the allocation. The operator is expected to weigh the advantages of the approach against its operational and scalability needs.

The RFC lists key requirements: advertise the capability, identify PCECC LSPs in messages, allow PCC-based label allocation, update or clean up downloaded labels, and synchronize labels between PCE and PCC.
sections.eli5: The boss owns a set of numbered stickers on each router and only the boss may use them. Sometimes the router is allowed to pick a sticker and tell the boss which one.

sections.title: Advertising PCECC Capability
sections.content:
During PCEP session setup, each side advertises PCECC support in its OPEN message with three elements: the new Path Setup Type (PST) 2 in the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV, a new PCECC-CAPABILITY sub-TLV with the L bit set to 1 for label download, and the STATEFUL-PCE-CAPABILITY TLV with the I flag set. Both sides must do this, otherwise the PCECC extensions MUST NOT be used.

The RFC defines error handling for mismatches, each followed by terminating the session:

  • PCECC sub-TLV present without the stateful capability or its I flag: Error-Type 19, Error-value 17.
  • PST 2 listed without the sub-TLV: Error-Type 10, Error-value 33.
  • A PCECC operation attempted without agreement: Error-Type 19, Error-value 16.

A sub-TLV that appears without PST 2 listed MUST be ignored. A legacy speaker ignores the unknown sub-TLV. If it later sees the unsupported PST in a request, it sends Error-Type 21, Error-value 1.
sections.eli5: Before working together, the two sides each hold up a card saying they know how to play this game. If one does not, they stop and say why.

sections.title: Setting Up a PCECC LSP
sections.content:
PCEP messages about a PCECC LSP MUST carry the PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV in the SRP object with PST set to 2. There are two ways to start an LSP.

In the PCE-initiated case, the PCE sends a PCInitiate message to the ingress PCC. The ingress answers with a PCRpt in the Going-up state, carrying the assigned PLSP-ID and with the D and C flags set. The PCE then assigns labels and sends a PCInitiate with a Central Controller Instruction (CCI) to each node along the path. Each node acknowledges with a PCRpt, and finally the PCE MUST send a PCUpd to the ingress.

In the PCC-initiated case, the PCC delegates the LSP with a PCRpt carrying PST 2 and the D flag. The PCE SHOULD calculate the path and then downloads labels in the same way. PCECC LSPs MUST be delegated to a PCE at all times.

A node learns its role from the O (out-label) bit of the CCI objects it receives: the ingress gets one with O set, a transit node gets an in-label and an out-label, and the egress gets one without O set. PCECC LSPs are considered up by default, and a data-plane check is left out of scope.
sections.eli5: The boss first asks the starting router to open the path, then walks down the line giving each router its own instructions, and last says that it can now be used.

sections.title: Updates, Cleanup and Label Allocation
sections.content:
To remove an LSP, the PCE sends a PCInitiate with the R (remove) flag in the SRP object to each node, and each PCC answers with a PCRpt. A PCC that does not recognize the label sends Error-Type 19, Error-value 18.

An LSP update uses make-before-break. The PCE first downloads new label instructions with new CC-IDs, then updates the ingress to switch traffic, and only after the ingress acknowledges does it clean up the former instructions.

If a PCE fails, instructions are not removed immediately: they are cleaned up when the State Timeout Interval timer expires, and a PCC MUST support CCI removal when that happens. A new PCE can take over by sending a PCInitiate with the SRP, LSP and CCI objects. State synchronization reuses the normal PCRpt-based procedure so that the PCE's view of the labels matches the PCC's.

For PCC-based allocation, the PCE sets the C flag in the CCI. A label value of 0 asks the PCC to choose, while a value n asks for that specific label. The PCC MUST report back with a PCRpt or a PCErr. A PCC can withdraw or change an assigned label with a PCRpt, and the PCE then cleans up the old label.
sections.eli5: To change the route, the boss puts up the new signs first, then points traffic to them, and only then takes down the old signs, so nobody gets lost.

sections.title: Messages and the CCI Object
sections.content:
The RFC extends two messages. PCInitiate gets a central-control form made of an SRP, an LSP and a list of CCI objects. PCRpt gets a similar report form with an optional SRP, an LSP and CCI objects. The LSP-IDENTIFIERS TLV MUST be present in the LSP object. A missing SRP, LSP or CCI object triggers a PCErr with Error-Type 6. The messages are defined with Routing Backus-Naur Form.

The new CCI object has Object-Class 44 and Object-Type 1 for an MPLS label. Its fields are the CC-ID (a PCEP-specific identifier that is unique within the PCE's scope and constant for the session, where 0 and 0xFFFFFFFF are reserved), reserved bits, a 16-bit Flags field, a 20-bit Label and further reserved bits, followed by optional TLVs.

Two flags are defined: O marks an out-label, which requires next-hop information, and C means the PCC allocates the label. The next-hop or local interface information is carried in IPV4-ADDRESS, IPV6-ADDRESS or UNNUMBERED-ENDPOINT TLVs from RFC 8779 and must be a directly connected address.
sections.eli5: Each instruction is a small form with a number for the instruction, a box for the label, and two tick boxes: one saying whether it is for going out, one saying who picks the label.

sections.title: PCECC Error Codes
sections.content:
Beyond the capability errors, the RFC adds a new Error-Type 31, PCECC failure, which a PCC uses when it rejects an instruction. It must include the SRP object so the PCE knows which PCInitiate it concerns.

A label outside the range set aside for the PCE gets Error-value 1. A failure to install the entry gets 2. A CCI with a wrong O bit pattern, for example no out-label at the ingress, or an invalid label, gets 3. A valid but unavailable requested label gets 4. Next-hop information the PCC cannot resolve gets 5.

Extra CCI objects beyond the expected ones for a role MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: When a router cannot follow an instruction, it sends back a numbered note that says which kind of problem it was.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A central controller concentrates risk: a central point of failure, denial of service, and a focus for interception of messages to individual network elements. The extension builds on existing PCEP messages, so the security considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 continue to apply, and TLS for PCEP is described in RFC 8253.

A malicious PCE has complete control over the labels on a PCC and can cause major harm. The RFC RECOMMENDS using this extension only on mutually authenticated, encrypted sessions between a PCE and PCCs in the same administrative authority. It also notes that a flood of messages is possible and points to the rate limit in RFC 8281.

A malicious PCC adds attack surface because the PCE must keep a replica of each label. Implementations are RECOMMENDED to limit the resources a single PCC can use.
sections.eli5: If the boss is tricked or turns bad, every router follows the wrong signs. So the boss and the routers should check each other's identity and talk in secret.

fields.name: CC-ID
fields.desc: PCEP-specific identifier for the instruction; 0 and 0xFFFFFFFF are reserved.

fields.name: Reserved1
fields.desc: Zero when sent; ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Includes the C bit (PCC allocation) and the O bit (out-label).

fields.name: Reserved2
fields.desc: Zero when sent; ignored on receipt.

items.label: Label out of range
items.desc: Label is outside the range set aside for the PCE.

items.label: Instruction failed
items.desc: The PCC failed to download the label entry.

items.label: Invalid CCI
items.desc: The CCI or its label is invalid.

items.label: Unable to allocate the specified CCI
items.desc: The label is valid but the PCC cannot allocate it.

items.label: Invalid next-hop information
items.desc: The PCC cannot resolve the next hop.
